newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Police halt students in Belgrade, Dini negotiates.
newsitem.headline: Police halt students in Belgrade, Dini negotiates.

text.p: Riot police blocked a student march in Belgrade on Thursday as an international mediator urged opposition parties, trying to drive Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic from power, to ease their demands.

Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini met Milosevic and leaders of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition separately to try to end more than three weeks of street upheaval since disputed elections on November 17.

More than 40,000 students and 100,000 Zajedno supporters were on the streets of the capital in a show of opposition to Milosevic, coinciding with Dini's intervention, that reversed a slackening of protests this week.
Police in riot armour halted an attempt by the students to march from central Belgrade to the exclusive Dedinje suburb where Milosevic and senior members of the government live.
They were stopped under the windows of the embassy of the United States which has threatened Milosevic with reprisals if he crushed the demonstrations with force.
Although the protests have been peaceful, the atmosphere was nervous as the students retreated and more police appeared in side streets along the march route.
Zajedno claimed the socialists cheated it of victory in the local elections in Belgrade and other towns.
Its demonstrations have demanded that Milosevic, Serbia's virtually unchallenged ruler for nine years, should quit power and that the socialists recognise the Zajedno victory.
Dini said the opposition should rethink its objectives and told reporters:
"Reinstatement of the results seems to me to be something that is not on the cards as the basis for dialogue between the parties. They must find a formula around the impasse."
He said he found both sides "have dug themselves firmly into the positions from which they started."

A Zajedno statement denied rumours it was conducting secret negotiations with Milosevic and opposition leader Vuk Draskovic said: "The first condition is that Mr Milosevic must respect the electoral will of the people and recognise the results of November 17. After that, we are ready for dialogue."
Political sources said it was unlikely that Milosevic would budge on possession of the capital though he might pacify Zajedno by handing over other towns.
The authorities have begun to take a tougher line since a young worker was arrested and beaten by police for carrying an effigy of Milosevic in prison garb at a march last week.
Belgrade actor Gojko Baletic who was arrested during Wednesday's demonstration suffered head and leg injuries before being released, his wife said.
Draskovic told demonstrators that police had been ordered to arrest and beat one person each day to intimidate the opposition.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher told CBS television that Milosevic would doom his hopes of ties with the West if he continued his "repressive, undemocratic stance".

The United States has considered re-imposing sanctions which would be a severe economic blow to Milosevic after the European Union's refusal of preferential trade privileges for Serbia because of the election conflict.

The West has not so far fleshed out in detail what reprisals it might inflict on Milosevic if he does not yield and Zajedno has objected to the renewal of sanctions which would hurt ordinary Serbs more than the government.

Milosevic is aware the the United States is unlikely to lift its veto on renewed International Monetary Fund membership (IMF) unless he made concessions to the opposition far beyond what would be acceptable to his socialist hardliners.
Independent Yugoslav economists have calculated that the Yugoslav economy could survive for up to two years even under sanctions.
